title: Does Deterministic Verification Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Configurations? A Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Evaluation of a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to measure whether adding a deterministic network verifier to a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces unsafe configuration applications relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. Execution used declared_model = gpt-5-mini, deterministic_netops_validator_v5, and shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial LLM generation per task reused across arms); guarded episodes could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial). Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms (baseline = 240/240 safe; guarded = 240/240 safe). The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate contract the single shared initial candidate passed deterministic validation in every task and no validator‑triggered repairs occurred (repair_attempts = 0), which mechanistically explains the degenerate paired contrast. We report the preregistered design, exact mapping to archived analysis outputs, an artifact‑grounded failure analysis of the null paired result, and concrete recommendations for informative future GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Automating translation of operator intent into device configurations is a core NetOps objective, and recent work shows LLMs can produce plausible configuration sequences but may violate execution‑time semantics (ordering, transient invariants, protected resources) that text metrics miss [1]. Emulation‑grounded, closed‑loop benchmarks expose such semantic failures by executing generated configs against device images and deterministic scorers [1]. The generate–validate–repair (GVR) pattern—LLM generation followed by deterministic verification and automated repair—aims to close this gap by preventing unsafe applies before execution [2,3]. Prior studies document GVR‑style benefits on selected fault classes, but empirical questions remain about verifier impact under distribution shift and adversarial prompts and about experimental designs that yield informative paired contrasts [2,4,6].

We preregistered and executed a confirmatory paired experiment to estimate a single, well‑defined estimand: the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline) under shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial LLM generation per task reused by both arms). The preregistration, execution traces, validator logs, and analysis artifacts are archived and constitute the evidentiary basis for every quantitative claim below. Our contributions are (1) an artifact‑grounded, preregistered paired GVR evaluation with N = 240 pairs; (2) an explicit mapping from preregistered estimand to archived analysis outputs (paired contingency table, bootstrap parameters, and reconciliation manifest); and (3) an evidence‑based failure analysis that explains the null paired outcome and yields concrete design recommendations for future informative GVR tests.
sections.related_work:
Executable, emulation‑grounded NetOps benchmarks and closed‑loop evaluation frameworks have been proposed to reveal planning and execution faults beyond text fidelity; NetConfArena is an explicit instance demonstrating how emulation uncovers multi‑device semantic failures [1]. Literature on automatic configuration repair and program repair documents generate–validate patterns and shows that validators often enable high syntactic repair coverage, with semantic coverage depending on verifier design and rule sets [2,4]. Survey and position papers synthesize agentic architectures, tool augmentation, and verifier integration as promising safety patterns but emphasize remaining gaps in calibration, verifier coverage, and adversary evaluation protocols [3,5]. The engineering evolution of tools such as Batfish provides an applied precedent for verifier design and incremental checking in networks [6].

This study differs from prior work by (a) preregistering a single paired estimand, (b) using shared_initial_candidate execution semantics (one shared LLM generation per task), (c) grounding scoring in deterministic emulator execution and validator traces, and (d) fully archiving per‑call traces, validator traces, and analysis outputs so the precise estimand is reproducibly reconcilable to archived artifacts. Our failure analysis and recommendations explicitly connect observed execution artifacts (provider_call_audit, validator_trace, deterministic_reconciliation.json) to design choices documented in the literature (validator coverage and paired design tradeoffs) and to open gaps identified in recent syntheses.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0dc935a8754bf2dfbe6869ff989c47f1db0d93e2ca34809be8ebf95e26). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate where unsafe_apply = 1 indicates a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation when applied). The analysis executor maps archived 'success' to safe_apply = 0; archived condition_summary reports baseline_success_count = 240 and guarded_success_count = 240, which correspond to baseline_unsafe_apply = 0 and guarded_unsafe_apply = 0.

Design and sampling: The design is paired with shared_initial_candidate semantics: exactly one initial LLM generation per task was produced and reused across both arms (provider_call_audit.hosted_model_call_event_count = 240; provider_call_audit.stage_counts.shared_initial_generation = 240). We executed N = 240 distinct intent→configuration tasks blocked into topology/vendor clusters: in‑distribution 60% (144), distribution‑shift 20% (48), adversarial 20% (48). Tasks were generated deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; representative task manifests are archived in the execution bundle.

Adapter contract, model, and verifier: Execution requested model gpt-5-mini and used adapter_family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and was permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. Under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics only a validator failure of the shared initial candidate or an invoked repair could create a discordant pair; the archive records repair_attempts = 0 and validation_after.valid = true for every task.

Scoring and exclusions: A deterministic emulator+validator produced a binary final outcome (safe = 0, unsafe = 1). The preregistration specified exclusions for 'possible false‑safe' items (validator PASS but emulator unsafe outcome) and infra failures after two retries; the execution produced no infra failures and no 'possible false‑safe' flags (contamination_summary.csv is empty). All analysis parameters (bootstrap_resamples = 10000, bootstrap_seed = 1729) and the exact analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1) are archived and were used without deviation.

Statistical analysis (registered): The primary analysis used the registered executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 to compute the paired contingency (n_11, n_10, n_01, n_00), the paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729), and an exact two‑sided McNemar test on discordant pairs. Secondary planned summaries included median repair counts and model‑call budgets; repair_attempts = 0 across archived repair logs.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting: The run completed per plan: planned_episode_count = 480, completed_episode_count = 480, complete_pair_count = 240, model_calls_used = 240, maximum_model_calls = 480. Provider call audit confirms a single shared initial generation per task (hosted_model_call_event_count = 240; cache_miss_count = 240; stage_counts.shared_initial_generation = 240). No infra failures or preregistered exclusions occurred.

Primary outcomes and contingency: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. The archived condition_summary.csv records baseline_successes = 240, baseline_failures = 0 and guarded_successes = 240, guarded_failures = 0. The paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is: n11 = 240; n10 = 0; n01 = 0; n00 = 0. Hence the paired estimate (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. The registered executor produced a bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (resamples = 10,000; seed = 1729) and exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; these numeric outputs are recorded in analysis/results.json and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl.

Validator and repair activity: Validator traces for representative tasks (execution/scoring/task-000004-*.json etc.) show validation_before.valid = true and validation_after.valid = true, violation_count = 0, and repair_applied = false. Across the full repair log repair_attempts = 0. deterministic_reconciliation.json records all_deterministic_consistency_checks_passed = true and confirms provider_call_audit consistency.

Planned but unused sensitivity channels: No 'possible false‑safe' flags were raised and no infra failures occurred; contamination_summary.csv is empty and missingness_summary.csv reports zero missing or excluded pairs. Planned subgroup contrasts (in‑distribution / shift / adversarial) are degenerate (all zeros) and slices of the archived contingency table show identical safety across subgroups.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded explanation for the null paired contrast: The preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced exactly one shared LLM output per task and the deterministic validator passed every shared candidate (validator_trace.valid = true for all tasks). Under the adapter contract the guarded arm could only change outcomes by invoking a validator‑triggered repair; because the validator did not flag any violations and no repairs were invoked (repair_attempts = 0), the guarded arm could not produce discordant pairs. This mechanistic chain (shared initial candidate → validator PASS → no repair) is fully traceable in provider_call_audit, validator_trace, and deterministic_reconciliation.json and explains the degenerate contingency (n_11 = 240, n_10 = n_01 = 0).

Design tradeoffs and implications: Shared_initial_candidate semantics yields clear advantages (direct pairing, reduced model‑call budget) but also conditions the paired contrast on initial candidate failures. When the initial generator is accurate or the verifier's rule set does not cover subtle semantic fault classes, the guarded arm cannot improve paired outcomes. Our execution artifacts show exactly this effect: a single shared generation per task, validator PASS in every task, and zero repair usage. To measure verifier causal impact in future work one should (a) permit independent initial generations per arm or explicitly inject generator variability, (b) increase adversary strength or expand adversarial protocols to create realistic generator failures, and/or (c) enlarge repair budgets and richer repair search strategies so the repair mechanism can be exercised when validation fails. These recommendations map directly to candidate gaps in the literature (G2,G3,G4) and to the execution manifest evidence that the guarded pipeline was never invoked to alter a final configuration.

Threats to validity (artifact‑grounded): Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate is an explicit design choice that restricts causal interpretation; execution manifests record adherence to that contract. Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite check set; validator traces include observed_touched_field_count and violation_codes but uncovered semantic fault classes may remain. External validity: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus and deterministic task generator; generalization to production multi‑vendor deployments is limited. Conclusion validity: the realized baseline unsafe rate = 0 precludes detecting verifier benefit under the chosen design and task corpus; power provisions in the preregistration assumed nonzero baseline risk and generator variability.

Relationship to prior work and open gaps: Prior repairs and verifier studies report improved repair coverage on injected or syntactic faults [2,4,6], but their measured benefits depend on fault generation and verifier coverage. Our null paired result highlights that an informative evaluation of GVR requires experimental arms and adversary protocols that produce opportunities for the verifier and repair components to act—an empirical gap consistent with the candidate_gaps identified in the evidence synthesis (G1–G4).
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a GVR pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Observed outcome: every paired episode was safe under both arms, yielding a paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). The archived execution artifacts explain this null paired contrast: the single shared initial LLM candidate passed deterministic_netops_validator_v5 in every task, no validator‑triggered repairs were applied (repair_attempts = 0), and therefore the guarded arm had no opportunity to create discordant (improved) outcomes. This result does not refute the potential utility of deterministic verification in other designs; rather it demonstrates how shared_initial_candidate semantics and verifier coverage jointly determine whether a paired experiment can measure verifier benefit. We provide concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations (allow independent initial generations, increase adversary strength, expand repair budgets, and broaden verifier checks) to enable future informative GVR evaluations. All preregistration, execution traces, validator logs, and analysis artifacts are archived and support the numeric claims reported here (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl, deterministic_reconciliation.json).

disclosure_statement: Models and orchestration: Execution used declared_model = "gpt-5-mini" via the registered adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. Runtime sampling: the archived model configuration records temperature = null (unset); unset temperature does not imply determinism by the hosted provider and sampling nondeterminism remains possible; all model‑call metadata were archived. Preregistration and autonomy: the study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0dc935a8754bf2dfbe6869ff989c47f1db0d93e2ca34809be8ebf95e26) and executed under the frozen plan after the autonomy lock. Human role and autonomy boundary: prior to the autonomy lock the human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt; all literature discovery, experiment design, preregistration, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting occurred autonomously after the lock per track rules. Generation semantics and causal contrast: the registered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms); therefore under the adapter contract only validator failures of the shared candidate or validator‑triggered repairs could create paired divergences. Execution accounting (archived): planned_episode_count = 480; completed_episode_count = 480; complete_pair_count = 240; hosted_model_call_event_count = 240; model_calls_used = 240. Immutable master prompt: archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). The execution archive contains preregistration, per‑call traces, validator traces, and analysis artifacts that substantiate the numeric outputs reported in the manuscript. No manual human editing of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompts, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.

Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected by the verifier, and validator PASS vs simulator outcome mismatches were planned to be flagged and analyzed (none occurred in this run).
